title: Granite 4.2: IBM's Open 3B/8B/30B Family
hook: Three Apache-2.0 dense models with 512K context, trained through a five-phase pretrain, agentic SFT, and stacked GRPO runs — with the whole recipe written down.
key_points: Three dense decoder-only models at 3B, 8B, and 30B, all with 512K-token context, released under Apache 2.0.
Standard modern stack: grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU feed-forward, RMSNorm, bfloat16.
Pretrained on roughly 15 trillion tokens across five phases of progressively higher data quality and longer context.
Supervised fine-tuning on 7.2M samples (~100B tokens), about 31.6% of it agentic instruction data.
Multi-stage RL: warm-started GRPO runs for verifiable-reward tasks, then agentic RL in sandboxed repos, shells, and web for 8B/30B, then RLHF.
Three reasoning modes — full thinking, low-effort thinking, and non-thinking — plus OpenAI-compatible tool calling.
content_html: IBM released Granite 4.2 as three dense, decoder-only models — 3B, 8B, and 30B — each with a 512K-token context window and an Apache 2.0 license. The architecture is deliberately unexotic: grouped-query attention, rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU feed-forward layers, RMSNorm, bfloat16. The value is in the recipe, which IBM wrote up in detail.
extra_html:
The pipeline

Pretraining ran roughly 15 trillion tokens across five phases, progressively raising data quality and extending context. Supervised fine-tuning used 7.2M samples — about 100B tokens — of which roughly a third was agentic instruction data. Then a sequence of warm-started GRPO runs: foundational RL with verifiable rewards on math, coding, and STEM; an agentic RL stage where the 8B and 30B train inside real sandboxed environments doing software engineering, terminal work, and web search; and a final RLHF alignment pass.

What you get

The models support native OpenAI-compatible tool calling, twelve languages, and three reasoning modes — full thinking, low-effort thinking, and non-thinking — so callers can trade reasoning tokens against latency. IBM reports the 30B at 33.29% on SWE Bench Pro against 19.11% for the 8B, and 89.17% on AIME25. As always with self-reported evals, the interesting part is the gap between sizes and the published methodology rather than the absolute figures.

flashcards.prompt: What are Granite 4.2's three reasoning modes?
flashcards.back_html: Full thinking, low-effort thinking, and non-thinking — letting a caller trade reasoning tokens against latency and cost per request.

flashcards.prompt: What distinguishes the agentic RL stage from the foundational RL stage in Granite 4.2's recipe?

choices.text: Agentic RL trains the 8B and 30B in real sandboxed environments — code repos, shells, web search
Agentic RL uses human preference labels instead of verifiable rewards
Agentic RL runs before pretraining finishes

flashcards.explanation_html: Foundational RL uses verifiable rewards on math, coding, and STEM; the agentic stage puts the larger models into real environments for software engineering, terminal work, and web search.

flashcards.prompt: Why does publishing a full training recipe matter for an open model release?
flashcards.back_html: Open weights alone are not reproducible — the phased data mix, SFT composition, and RL staging are what let others replicate or adapt the result.
